1b5f5720-5def-48c8-a293-f145dc86305a.recap: The piece argues the private-credit stress that surfaced with Tricolor and First Brands roughly a year ago never resolved, it just moved slower and out of headlines. Blackstone's BCRED, the largest non-traded BDC (~$77bn AUM), has capped repurchases at 5% for a second straight quarter even as shareholders requested ~10% withdrawals, and its NAV slipped from $24.68 to $23.64 per share between January and July. Across tracked private-credit funds, investors sought $23bn in Q2 redemptions, leaving an estimated $15bn backlog, while non-traded BDC fundraising fell 82% year-on-year to ~$2bn, the lowest since 2020. Public BDC portfolios have now contracted for three straight quarters as repayments outpace new originations. In public credit, CCC-rated junk spreads have widened to 1,053bp, matching stress levels last seen in the April 2025 tariff shock and August 2024 yen-carry unwind, even as IG and higher-quality HY stay calm — a divergence the host reads as the market pricing real refinancing risk at the bottom of the credit stack. The story then widens geographically and thematically: Australian builder Bathla collapsed under roughly AU$3.3bn of private-credit debt (mostly floating-rate, from 40+ lenders), triggering redemption gates at several Australian private-credit funds; separately, iron-ore trader Radiant World is under investigation (with a Jefferies-linked fund and Glencore exposed) over allegedly fraudulent invoices used as financing collateral, echoing the Tricolor/First Brands pattern in trade finance rather than direct lending.

313bf49f-b6bf-4487-894b-2f71ac944c88.one_liner: A consumer-economy deep dive (Circle K, Walmart, US Open ticket resales, construction spending, JOLTS/ADP) arguing an energy-price shock is masking underlying demand destruction and labor-market weakness -- relevant macro backdrop for the Fed's rate path rather than a funding-market story.
313bf49f-b6bf-4487-894b-2f71ac944c88.recap: The host (in a Jeff Snyder/Eurodollar-style commentary) argues that headline consumer resilience is illusory once you look past nominal spending totals. Circle K's parent Alimentation Couche-Tard reported record fuel revenue (+33% YoY, $16.7bn) driven purely by higher oil prices, even as same-store fuel volumes fell 1.6% in the US and 4.3% in Europe -- rising dollars, falling gallons, the textbook signature of demand destruction. Store traffic and discretionary merchandise sales (snacks, drinks) also softened, with management citing 'increasingly intentional' spending. The same pattern shows up elsewhere: US Open resale ticket prices collapsed 50-88% in the days before sessions (unusual versus last year's late run-up); Walmart cut prices on 11,000 items while basket size shrank; Kroger, Amazon and Aldi are pushing into discounting, suggesting a brewing grocery price war; and higher-income households are trading down into Dollar General while Dollar Tree's traffic barely moved. On labor, ADP and JOLTS data (hiring near 5.1mn, falling quits) contradict the stronger BLS payroll print, and Uber is cutting 3,300 jobs (~10% of staff). The centerpiece argument is construction spending: both non-residential and residential construction have been contracting since late 2023/September 2025 respectively, despite lower market rates -- proof, the host argues, that falling rates reflect weakening growth expectations rather than acting as stimulus. The conclusion: an energy shock is transferring purchasing power to energy producers while destroying demand everywhere else, not igniting broad inflation.

a9265c2e-d86c-4d49-9344-7643e5e1274d.one_liner: A Macrohive strategist lays out a K-shaped, low-hire/low-fire US economy, argues AI-chip prices are a hidden supply shock keeping inflation sticky, and reads the FOMC's internal politics as tilting toward one more hike this year before cuts in 2027.
a9265c2e-d86c-4d49-9344-7643e5e1274d.recap: Macrohive strategist Dominique Dwor-Frecaut characterizes the US economy as full-employment but fragile and K-shaped: aggregate growth and consumption look fine, but non-mortgage consumer debt is deleveraging, delinquencies on credit cards/autos/student loans rival GFC levels, and the savings rate has fallen to near pre-GFC lows to sustain spending amid flat real incomes. She attributes stable Okun's-law dynamics (coefficient near 2) to a 'low-hire, low-fire' labor market driven by weak labor supply and AI-induced hiring caution, evidenced by a falling job-finding rate and rising unemployment duration despite low unemployment. On inflation, she argues the surge in AI-driven chip prices is an underappreciated supply shock analogous to an energy shock, which the FOMC has misread as demand pressure; a flat Phillips curve means these shocks aren't feeding into wages, keeping core trend measures (trimmed-mean, median CPI/PCE) on a gentle downward path. On the Fed, she describes a structural shift from a chair-centric FOMC (Bernanke/Yellen/Powell) to open dissent under Chair Warsh, requiring tracking of every voter rather than a few 'chair whisperers.' Despite Warsh's hawkish rhetoric on five-year-high inflation, she expects the committee dynamics (contingent on a pivotal Waller speech) could produce one more hike this year, followed by cuts in 2027 assuming no new supply shocks. She also flags Treasury Secretary Bessent's remarks about potential bank-bond purchases as a signal to asset managers, against a backdrop of a 6% deficit, debt/GDP above 100%, and a proposed 50% military budget increase, all bearish for the long end. Her surprise scenario for 2027 is that AI capex growth stalls with smaller-than-expected fallout for GDP, partly because much of the capex is import-leakage rather than domestic demand.
terms: Okun's law -- empirical relationship between GDP growth and changes in the unemployment rate
FOMC -- Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's rate-setting body
PCE -- Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge
r-star -- the theoretical neutral real interest rate consistent with stable inflation and full employment
